findings.title: Async legacy writes are canceled when the request context ends
findings.body: In Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its 10s-timeout context from the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). As soon as the API request returns, the request context is canceled, so the deferred legacy write/delete is aborted with 'context canceled' rather than running for its timeout. This defeats the stated purpose of the mode ('write to legacy as a safe measure') and silently leaves the two stores divergent. The goroutines should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or background) as the parent.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records legacy result with the storage metrics recorder
findings.body: In DeleteCollection's goroutine, the outcome of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latencies and failures are therefore attributed to unified storage, corrupting the dual-writer metrics used to monitor migration progress.

findings.title: Delete records 'name' where the resource 'kind' label is expected
findings.body: On success, Delete calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passing the object name as the label where every other call passes `options.Kind`. This produces unbounded/high-cardinality metric label values (one per object name) and inconsistent series compared to the failure path on line 103 which uses options.Kind.

findings.title: Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy metrics
findings.body: When d.Storage.Create fails (line 45) or d.Storage.Update fails (line 129), the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the legacy store was never contacted. These failures and their durations are attributed to legacy storage, skewing the dual-writer observability data. Both should be recordStorageDuration.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are swallowed with no logging or reconciliation
findings.body: Previously, errors from the legacy store were at least logged. In the new goroutines, the error from d.Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is only converted into a boolean for a metric; it is never logged and no reconciliation/retry is queued. Since mode 3 is the last dual-write stage before cutting over to unified storage, silent legacy failures mean data loss in the legacy store with no operator-visible signal beyond an aggregate counter and no way to recover the missed write.

findings.title: Legacy Update reuses the request's objInfo, so legacy can write different data than storage
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo so the legacy store received exactly the object that unified storage wrote (via updateWrapper). The new code passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update in a goroutine, so the legacy store re-computes the updated object from its own (possibly stale) current state. If legacy and unified have diverged (e.g., an earlier async legacy write was canceled or failed), the legacy copy can end up with different content than the authoritative unified copy. The updateWrapper mechanism was removed without a replacement guarantee.

findings.title: Legacy Delete failures on NotFound are treated as errors
findings.body: The old Delete tolerated apierrors.IsNotFound from the legacy store (expected when an object exists only in unified storage, which is the common case in mode 3 after migration backfill gaps). The new code records any legacy Delete error, including NotFound, as a failure metric. In mode 3, objects created before backfill will routinely 404 in legacy, producing persistent false failure signals.

findings.title: Delete logs with the bare logger, dropping name/kind context
findings.body: In Delete, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` is used instead of the `log` variable built two lines above (which includes name, kind and method). Any error logged in Delete will lack the identifying fields, unlike every other method in this file. Likely a copy-paste oversight.

findings.title: Unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens
findings.body: Mode 3's defining behavior is 'write to unified, then asynchronously write to legacy', but none of the tests assert that Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection are invoked (e.g., via m.AssertExpectations or waiting on the goroutine with mock.AssertEventually). The tests return immediately after the unified call, so the goroutines may not have run; a regression that drops the legacy write entirely (or is canceled immediately, as in the context bug) would still pass. Also the error-path test cases set up legacy mock expectations that are never exercised or verified.

findings.title: TestMode3_Get creates its own registry instead of the shared one
findings.body: TestMode3_Get declares a local `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` while every other mode-3 test uses the package-level `p`. This is inconsistent and, if the dual writer registers metrics in NewDualWriter, would panic on double registration in other tests or mask registration issues; the unrelated change to TestMode1_Get that moved `p` to package scope suggests this local declaration is an oversight.
